slides.title: Applying Exponent Laws
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is today's move: a negative fraction's reciprocal is negative. A board with 5/2 (sign dropped) or 2/5 (opposite of the opposite) is the error this lesson is built to catch — the B1G-M lists 'takes the opposite instead of the reciprocal' as the misconception for this benchmark.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Each row is the previous row divided by 2/5, which is multiplying by 5/2. Going down from (2/5)⁰ = 1: 1 · 5/2 = 5/2, then 25/4, then 125/8. Students see that (2/5)⁻¹ is 5/2 — the reciprocal — before the rule is stated.
OFF: 'To divide by two fifths you multiply by five halves. That is why the base flips.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
State the rule and then the reason: (a/b)⁻ⁿ = 1/(a/b)ⁿ = 1 ÷ aⁿ/bⁿ = bⁿ/aⁿ = (b/a)ⁿ. Then the sign question: (−2/3)⁻⁵ is (−3/2)⁵ — the minus rides along with the fraction. A student who writes (2/3)⁵ took the opposite AND the reciprocal, which is the named misconception.
OFF: 'Reciprocal flips top and bottom. It does not touch the sign.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Fernanda: quotient of powers first, then power of a power, then rewrite the decimal as a fraction and flip. Junior: power of a quotient first, then quotient. Both land on (2/5)². The decimal-to-fraction step is the one to watch: 2.5 = 5/2, so (2.5)⁻² = (5/2)⁻² = (2/5)².

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. What is the base? What does the negative exponent tell you to do to it? Do the numbers or the sign flip?

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Flip: (−8/7)². Square: 64/49. Even power, so positive. A board with −64/49 squared only the numerator's magnitude and kept a sign; a board with 49/64 never flipped.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who flips the sign with the fraction (the answer here is negative, and a board with +8/125 dropped it) and one who never flipped (−125/8). −8/125 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Same base twice — which law joins them? What is the exponent after that, and what does its sign tell you?

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Product of powers: −2 + 4 = 2. The exponent is already positive, so no flip. Value 25/64. The trap is flipping anyway because a negative exponent appeared somewhere in the problem.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who adds to −1 and stops there (a negative exponent is not a finished answer), and one who writes (5/4)¹⁰ (added 7 + 3 but kept the minus). (4/5)¹⁰ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: The rule, plain. A board with (2/3)⁴ dropped the minus without flipping; a board with −(3/2)⁴ made the exponent's sign the value's sign.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Sign inside the denominator. A board with (5/3)⁹ took the opposite as well as the reciprocal — the named misconception.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Note that A and B have the SAME VALUE (64/49) because the power is even — a student who chooses B for that reason is right about the value and wrong about the law. Ask them to redo it with exponent −3, where B would be wrong in value too.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. −2 − (−4) = 2. The B board is the interesting one: it did the arithmetic right and then flipped out of habit.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Two bases that are reciprocals of each other: flip the first and they match. A board with 1 multiplied 2/5 by 5/2 and forgot the exponent flipped the first factor.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Product then power of a power: (5 − 2) · 3 = 9. A board with (2/3)²¹ multiplied 5 · −2 · 3 wrongly; (2/3)⁶ added 3 + 3.

slides.note: Written. This is the misconception the state guide names for this benchmark, in the student's own words. Full credit: the correct rewrite and a sentence that separates reciprocal from opposite. Value, if anyone asks: −243/32.
